issues.legal_issue: Consideration received for surrender of a tenancy right is not chargeable as capital gains when the acquisition cost cannot be ascertained under the applicable computation rules.
material_facts: The assessee held leasehold tenancy rights under a long-term lease and surrendered them to the lessor before the lease expired.
The lessor paid the assessee consideration for the surrender.
The Department's position before the High Court was that the cost of acquiring the tenancy rights could not be ascertained.
The applicable law did not provide that the acquisition cost of the tenancy rights was to be treated as nil.
issues.conclusion: The receipt was not chargeable to capital gains because the computation required by Section 48 could not be applied where the acquisition cost was unascertainable.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 45 and 48 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 operate together: a transfer is not chargeable under Section 45 if the prescribed computation under Section 48 cannot be made. Under Commissioner of Income Tax v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty, an asset whose acquisition cost cannot be determined under the applicable law falls outside the capital-gains charge. A tenancy right may in principle have an ascertainable acquisition cost, as recognised in A.R. Krishnamurthy v. Commissioner of Income Tax, but the Department's position in this case was that the cost could not be ascertained. The later amendment to Section 55(2), which provided for a nil cost for tenancy rights, did not apply to the assessment in issue.

rule.if: income_tax_chargeability_appeal and tenancy_right_transferred_for_consideration and acquisition_cost_unascertainable and cost_not_deemed_nil_by_applicable_law

predicates.income_tax_chargeability_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning whether a receipt is chargeable to income tax.
predicates.tenancy_right_transferred_for_considerat: A taxpayer transferred or surrendered a tenancy right and received consideration for it.
predicates.acquisition_cost_unascertainable: The acquisition cost of the transferred tenancy right cannot be ascertained for the required computation.

issues.definition: When an income-tax chargeability appeal concerns consideration for a tenancy-right transfer, and its acquisition cost cannot be ascertained or treated as nil under the applicable law, the capital-gains charge does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A receipt arising from the transfer of a capital asset that is classified under the capital-gains head cannot be taxed under the residuary head merely because the capital-gains computation cannot be made.
material_facts: The receipt arose from surrendering tenancy rights, which were accepted to be a capital asset, and was a capital receipt.
The Department sought to tax the receipt as income from other sources if it could not be taxed as capital gains.
The capital-gains charge did not apply because the acquisition cost could not be ascertained under the applicable computation rules.
issues.conclusion: The receipt could not be taxed as income from other sources under Sections 10(3) and 56; if it could not be taxed under Section 45, it could not be taxed at all.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14 classifies income under distinct heads, and Section 56 applies only to income not chargeable under another specified head. Income that falls within the capital-gains head cannot be shifted to the residuary head because the capital-gains computation fails. The Court relied on United Commercial Bank Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, East India Housing and Land Development Trust Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Commissioner of Income Tax v. Chugandas and Co., S.G. Mercantile Corporation (P) Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, and Nalinikant Ambalal Mody v. S.A.L. Narayan Row, CIT.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a receipt from a capital-asset transfer that belongs to the capital-gains head but cannot be charged there, the receipt cannot instead be taxed under the residuary head.
